overview.title: Fine-tuning results: 98.6% test accuracy
overview.main_topic: Running the fine-tuning fit (end of Listing 8.31), evaluating the best checkpoint on the test set, figure 8.15, and putting the 98.6% result in context.
overview.central_idea: Fine-tuning the Xception base with augmentation for 30 epochs at a 1e-5 learning rate gives a test accuracy of 98.6%, the best result of the chapter, achieved with about 10% of the data available in the original Kaggle competition, though helped by pretrained knowledge about cats and dogs.

summary:
The page finishes **Listing 8.31**: `model.fit` on `augmented_train_dataset` for **30 epochs**, with `validation_dataset` and the `ModelCheckpoint` callbacks defined on p.289. Then the best checkpoint is reloaded with `keras.models.load_model("fine_tuning.keras")` and evaluated on `test_dataset`, printing the accuracy with three decimals.

**Figure 8.15** shows the training and validation metrics for fine-tuning. Both accuracy curves start at about 0.982, the level the feature-extraction model had already reached. Validation accuracy climbs slowly and steadily to about 0.987; training accuracy fluctuates between roughly 0.985 and 0.997. Validation loss decreases smoothly from about 0.052 to about 0.043; training loss is noisy, between about 0.015 and 0.035. The y-axis ranges are very narrow: these are small refinements of an already strong model.

The **test accuracy is 98.6%** (results may vary by about half a percentage point). In the original Kaggle dogs-vs-cats competition this would have been one of the top results, but the authors flag that the comparison is not fair: the pretrained features already contained prior knowledge about cats and dogs, which competitors in 2013 could not use.

On the positive side, the result uses only **about 10%** of the training data that was available in the competition: 2,000 vs 20,000 samples. The page ends by noting that you now have a solid toolbox for image classification, especially with small datasets: training from scratch with augmentation, feature extraction, and fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning
concepts.definition: Unfreezing a pretrained base and jointly training it with an already trained head, at a low learning rate.
concepts.intuition: A final polish of an already strong model.
concepts.technical: 30 epochs, augmented data, Adam(1e-5), best checkpoint by val_loss.
concepts.significance: Best result of the chapter: 98.6% test accuracy.
concepts.misconception: Fine-tuning gives large jumps in accuracy; here it adds about 0.2 points over feature extraction with augmentation.

concepts.name: Model checkpointing and best-model selection
concepts.definition: Saving the model during training when the validation metric improves, and reloading that best version for evaluation.
concepts.intuition: Keep the best draft, not just the last one.
concepts.significance: Protects against late-epoch overfitting without needing to pick the number of epochs exactly.
concepts.misconception: After fit returns, model already holds the best weights; it holds the last epoch's weights unless you reload.

concepts.name: Transfer learning and data efficiency
concepts.definition: Reusing knowledge learned on a large dataset to solve a new task with little data.
concepts.intuition: Most of the learning happened on ImageNet; the new task only needs a little.
concepts.significance: About 10% of the competition's data suffices for a top-level result.
concepts.misconception: The model truly learned from only 2,000 images; it also carries knowledge from ImageNet's 1.4 million images (p.280).

concepts.name: Test set evaluation
concepts.definition: A final evaluation on data never used for training or model selection.
concepts.intuition: The exam you only sit once.
concepts.misconception: Validation accuracy and test accuracy are interchangeable; validation is used to make choices, so it is optimistically biased (p.135).

deeper.title: The whole chapter in one table
deeper.body:
| Approach | Test accuracy | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Small ConvNet from scratch | 78.6% | p.276 |
| From scratch + data augmentation | about 84% (announced) | p.266 |
| Feature extraction + augmentation (frozen Xception) | 98.4% | p.288 |
| Fine-tuning Xception | 98.6% | p.290 |

The big jump comes from using a pretrained model at all (about +14 points). Fine-tuning adds a final, small improvement, within the half-point variance the authors mention. For reference, the best 2013 Kaggle entries reached up to 95% (p.268) using the full dataset but no ImageNet pretraining.

deeper.title: Comparing figures 8.14 and 8.15
deeper.body:
1. **Starting point.** Figure 8.15 starts at ~0.982 accuracy, which is where the feature-extraction model already was: fine-tuning begins from the trained head (steps 1-3 of p.288).
2. **Validation loss.** In figure 8.14 it hovered around 0.05 with spikes up to ~0.075; in figure 8.15 it falls steadily to ~0.043. Unfreezing the base lets the model keep improving on validation data.
3. **Training vs validation.** In 8.14 training accuracy was mostly *below* validation (frozen features, augmented inputs). In 8.15 it is *above* validation (~0.99 vs ~0.987): the base now adapts to the training images, so a small generalization gap appears.
4. **Stability.** The validation curve in 8.15 is much smoother, consistent with the tiny 1e-5 updates.

These readings are AI-written interpretations of the plots.

deeper.title: Why 'unfair' matters
deeper.body: When you compare a transfer-learning model with models trained from scratch, part of the advantage comes from the pretraining dataset. Here ImageNet contains many dog and cat images (p.285), so the pretrained base had seen exactly the kind of knowledge needed. On a domain far from ImageNet (satellite images, medical scans) you should expect a smaller boost. This is an AI elaboration on the book's caveat.

questions.question: Why does the evaluation code call keras.models.load_model("fine_tuning.keras") before evaluate?
options: Because fit deletes the model from memory.
To evaluate the epoch with the lowest validation loss rather than the last epoch.
To reset the base to its pretrained ImageNet weights.
Because evaluate only works on models loaded from disk.
questions.answer: To evaluate the epoch with the lowest validation loss rather than the last epoch.
questions.explanation: ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only=True and monitor="val_loss" (p.289) writes the best epoch to that file. fit does not delete the model, loading does not restore ImageNet weights, and evaluate works on any compiled model.

questions.question: What test accuracy does fine-tuning reach, and how much variation do the authors say to expect?
questions.answer: 98.6%, with your own results possibly within half a percentage point.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after figure 8.15.

questions.question: Why do the authors say the comparison with the original Kaggle competition is 'not quite a fair comparison'?
questions.answer: Because the pretrained features already contained prior knowledge about cats and dogs (ImageNet has many such images), which competitors couldn't use at the time.
questions.explanation: The page gives this reason; p.285 notes ImageNet contains many dog and cat instances.

questions.question: The test set has 2,000 images (p.265). Roughly how many images does a 98.6% model misclassify, and how many more does a 98.4% model misclassify?
questions.answer: About 28 errors at 98.6% (1.4% of 2,000); about 32 at 98.4%; so about 4 more images.
questions.explanation: $0.014 \times 2000 = 28$ and $0.016 \times 2000 = 32$. A 4-image difference is smaller than the ±0.5-point (±10 images) variance the authors mention.

questions.question: In figure 8.15 training accuracy is above validation accuracy, whereas in figure 8.14 it was mostly below. What changed?
questions.answer: The base is now trainable, so the model adapts its features to the training images and fits them slightly better than unseen validation images; with a frozen base, the harder augmented training inputs kept training accuracy below validation.
questions.explanation: An interpretation of the two figures (p.288 and this page), not stated in the book.

questions.question: What fraction of the data available in the Kaggle competition did the fine-tuned model use for training?
questions.explanation: The book says 2,000 samples versus 20,000, about 10%. The other options don't match those figures.

questions.question: Can you list the chapter's three strategies for small-data image classification and the test accuracy each reached?
questions.answer: From scratch (78.6%, about 84% with augmentation), feature extraction with a pretrained model (~98%, 98.4% with augmentation), fine-tuning (98.6%).
